description: Structured mapping of standardized symptoms (FEVER, COUGH, STOMACH_PAIN, etc.) to conditions, evidence, and red flags

conditions.name: Viral Upper Respiratory Tract Infection (Common Cold / Pharyngitis)
supportingEvidence: Concurrent nasal congestion, rhinitis, and upper airway irritation
Acute self-limiting onset without focal lung consolidation
contradictingEvidence: Severe pleuritic chest pain or focal rales on auscultation
redFlags: SpO2 dropping below 94%
Severe respiratory distress (stridor or gasping)
Inability to swallow liquids or drooling
Altered mental status or extreme lethargy
missingInformation: Accurate oral or axillary temperature measurement
Presence of earache or sinus facial pain
conditions.reasoning: The combination of cough, nasal discharge, and mild fever indicates acute viral involvement of the nasopharynx and upper respiratory tract.
conditions.recommendedNextStep: Rest, oral hydration, warm saline gargles, and steam inhalation. Seek formal clinical evaluation if fever persists beyond 3 days or breathing difficulty develops.

conditions.name: Influenza-like Illness (ILI)
supportingEvidence: Acute onset of fever with cough and marked systemic fatigue
contradictingEvidence: Localized acute abdominal tenderness or peritoneal irritation
Clear productive purulent sputum with lobar consolidation signs
Absence of fever throughout illness course
redFlags: Chest pain or cyanosis (blue lips/face)
Confusion or delirium during fever spikes
Hemoptysis (coughing up blood)
Persistent vomiting causing dehydration
missingInformation: Exact duration in hours or days
Resting respiratory rate and pulse oximetry reading
conditions.reasoning: Acute co-occurrence of high fever and dry or productive cough suggests an acute influenza-like respiratory syndrome requiring close monitoring.
conditions.recommendedNextStep: Prioritize bed rest and aggressive oral fluid replacement. Consult a primary care physician if fever exceeds 102°F or breathlessness emerges.

conditions.name: Acute Gastroenteritis / Enteritis
supportingEvidence: Crampy abdominal discomfort with loose watery stools or vomiting
History of questionable food or water ingestion
Acute onset (<72 hours) with diffuse periumbilical pain
contradictingEvidence: Localized sharp right lower quadrant pain with rebound tenderness (Appendicitis)
Rigid 'board-like' abdomen or absent bowel sounds (Perforation)
Gross rectal hemorrhage or black tarry stools (Melena)
redFlags: Severe signs of dehydration (sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, no urine >8 hours)
Intractable vomiting preventing any oral hydration
Blood or mucus in stool / Coffee-ground vomitus
Severe localized abdominal rigidity or guarding
missingInformation: Frequency of loose stools in last 24 hours
Ability to retain Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) solution
Presence of fever or visible blood in stools
conditions.reasoning: Abdominal cramping accompanied by emesis or loose motions strongly points toward acute infectious or toxin-mediated enteritis.
conditions.recommendedNextStep: Begin immediate Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) solution after every loose motion. Present to clinic or PHC for antiemetic/hydration assessment if unable to retain fluids.

conditions.name: Acute Gastritis / Acid Peptic Dyspepsia
supportingEvidence: Epigastric burning or gnawing ache related to meals or empty stomach
Recent intake of NSAID pain relievers, spicy food, or fasting
contradictingEvidence: Watery diarrhea or high spikes in body temperature
Radiation to left shoulder or jaw (must rule out inferior wall MI)
Unintentional significant weight loss or dysphagia
redFlags: Hematemesis (vomiting blood) or coffee-ground emesis
Black tarry stools (melena)
Severe crushing epigastric pain radiating to back (Pancreatitis)
Post-prandial syncope
missingInformation: Exact anatomical location of abdominal pain (epigastric vs lower quadrants)
History of NSAID use or past peptic ulcer disease
Relationship of pain to food intake (relief vs exacerbation)
conditions.reasoning: Epigastric discomfort and nausea without diarrhea or peritoneal signs is consistent with acid-peptic inflammation.
conditions.recommendedNextStep: Small frequent bland meals, avoid NSAID analgesics, and consult a doctor for clinical confirmation and acid suppression therapy.

conditions.name: Acute Undifferentiated Tropical Febrile Illness (Dengue / Malaria Suspect)
supportingEvidence: High-grade continuous or intermittent fever with intense retro-orbital or frontal headache
Severe body ache, arthralgia, or flushed appearance
Residence or travel in vector-borne endemic area
contradictingEvidence: Prominent upper airway coryza or productive purulent sputum
Fever duration exceeding 14 days without acute toxic signs
redFlags: Spontaneous mucosal bleeding (petechiae, bleeding gums, nosebleed)
Persistent severe abdominal pain and persistent vomiting
Clinical fluid accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion)
Postural dizziness, cold clammy extremities, or hypotension (Dengue Shock)
missingInformation: Day of fever illness (critical: days 3 to 7 are the critical phase)
Platelet count and hematocrit via CBC
Rapid diagnostic test (NS1 antigen / Malaria smear)
conditions.reasoning: Acute high fever coupled with retro-orbital headache and systemic discomfort requires close clinical observation and laboratory workup for tropical infections.
conditions.recommendedNextStep: Avoid Aspirin, Ibuprofen, or other NSAIDs (due to bleeding risk). Stay well hydrated with coconut water, ORS, and juices. Visit PHC or hospital for CBC and antigen tests immediately.
